concepts.title: Passes and Comparisons in Bubble Sort
concepts.definition: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent pairs and swaps unordered ones, needing n minus 1 passes for n elements; the pass number i makes n minus i minus 1 comparisons, so the whole sort spends n times n minus 1 over 2 comparisons.
concepts.key_idea: Each pass bubbles the largest remaining element to the end, so later passes shrink by one comparison.
question_patterns: How many passes and how many comparisons does bubble sort make on a 6-element list?

solution_steps.explain: A list of n elements needs n minus 1 passes.
Pass lengths n, n-1, ..., 1 sum to passes times n over 2.

worked_examples.q: Bubble sorting 6 elements needs how many passes?

concepts.title: Percentile Index from Sorted Marks
concepts.definition: An xth percentile answers the question 'better than what share of the class': after sorting the marks, multiply x percent by the number of students, round to a whole index, and read the mark stored there.
concepts.key_idea: The 90th percentile of 120 students sits at index 108 because 0.90 times 120 equals 108.

solution_steps.explain: Multiply by the number of values to land on the index.

concepts.title: Median of an Even List
concepts.definition: After a list is sorted, its median is the middle value; when the count is even, the two central values are added and halved, which is the value a bubble-sorted list hands to the median function.
concepts.key_idea: Sorting first is what makes the two middle positions meaningful for the median.
question_patterns: A sorted six-element list has 4 and 7 in the middle. Compute its median.

solution_steps.explain: Both central values participate in an even-length median.
The median is the average of the pair.

concepts.title: Quadratic Time of Nested Loops
concepts.definition: Loop-free algorithms run in constant time, a single loop costs linear time, and a loop inside a loop costs quadratic time; since all three sorts of this chapter nest one loop in another, each runs in order n squared.
concepts.key_idea: When a nested loop and a single loop coexist, the nested loop alone fixes the complexity class.
question_patterns: What is the time complexity of bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort, and why?

solution_steps.explain: A single pass touches each element once.
An inner loop over every element for every element gives the square.

worked_examples.q: A loop nested inside a loop over n elements costs order n to which power?

concepts.title: Bubble Sort Pass by Pass
concepts.definition: Working left to right, bubble sort compares each pair of neighbours and swaps them when the left one is larger, so after pass 1 of [8, 7, 13, 1, -9, 4] the 13 sits at the end, and the list finishes as -9, 1, 4, 7, 8, 13.
concepts.formula: if list1[j] > list1[j+1] then swap the pair
concepts.key_idea: A full pass with no swap proves the list is already sorted, so the algorithm may stop early.
question_patterns: Show the list [8, 7, 13, 1, -9, 4] after each of the first three bubble sort passes.
What does the list look like after pass 1, and which element has reached its final place?
How can bubble sort detect that the list is sorted before all passes finish?
Trace the swaps of pass 2 for the list of Figure 5.1.
Modify Algorithm 5.1 to sort a list in descending order.

solution_steps.action: walk the comparisons of each pass
solution_steps.explain: Compare neighbours from index 0, swap when the left value is bigger, and observe the largest remaining element settle at the right end after every pass.

worked_examples.q: In bubble sort, a pair is swapped when the left element is what relative to the right one?

concepts.title: Selection Sort Minimum Swaps
concepts.definition: Selection sort splits the list into a sorted left part and an unsorted right part, scans the unsorted part for its smallest element, and swaps that minimum with the leftmost unsorted slot, so at most one swap happens per pass for n minus 1 passes.
concepts.key_idea: After four passes on [7, 11, 3, 10, 17, 23, 1, 4, 21, 5] the four smallest values 1, 3, 4 and 5 already lead the list.
question_patterns: How many swaps at most does selection sort make while sorting n elements?
Determine the partially sorted list after four passes of selection sort on randList = [7, 11, 3, 10, 17, 23, 1, 4, 21, 5].
Why does selection sort usually make fewer swaps than bubble sort for the same list?
What do the variables min and flag do in Algorithm 5.2?
Sort the list 63, 42, 21, 9 with selection sort and count the swaps.

solution_steps.explain: Each pass finds the minimum of the unsorted region and swaps it into the boundary slot, growing the sorted prefix by exactly one element.

worked_examples.q: At most how many swaps happen in one selection-sort pass?

concepts.title: Insertion Sort Shifting
concepts.definition: Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix and pulls the first unsorted element aside in temp; it walks the prefix backwards shifting larger elements one place right, then drops temp into the gap, much like arranging playing cards in hand.
concepts.formula: while j >= 0 and temp < list3[j]: shift right, then insert
concepts.key_idea: Already-sorted input makes insertion sort cheapest, since no shifting is needed at all.
question_patterns: Show the list after each of the first three passes of insertion sort on [7, 11, 3, 10, 17, 23, 1, 4, 21, 5].
Why does insertion sort compare the new element with the sorted part from the backward direction?
Which of List 1 [2, 3, 5, 7, 11] and List 2 [11, 7, 5, 3, 2] needs fewer comparisons in insertion sort, and why?
What role does the variable temp play in Algorithm 5.3?
During admission, names are inserted in ascending order as they arrive. Which sorting technique is this?
Trace the shifts made when 1 is inserted into the sorted prefix 7, 11, 13.

solution_steps.explain: Each pass lifts one unsorted element, slides every larger sorted element right by one, and settles the lifted element into the vacancy.

worked_examples.q: Which sort keeps a sorted prefix and pulls the first unsorted element aside in temp?
